Common reasons ultrasound resolution exceeds (is worse than) theoretical values:

1. **Transducer bandwidth limitations** — Real transducers have finite bandwidth; if the actual center frequency or pulse duration differs from assumed values, axial resolution degrades.

2. **Near-field/far-field mismatch** — Theoretical lateral resolution assumes you're at the focal depth. Off-focus regions have significantly broader beam width.

3. **Beam divergence and side lobes** — Real beams aren't ideal; grating lobes and side lobes broaden the effective point spread function.

4. **Coupling and attenuation** — Poor acoustic coupling or frequency-dependent attenuation shifts the effective frequency lower, worsening resolution.

5. **Signal processing chain** — Envelope detection, filtering, or digitization (insufficient sampling rate) can broaden features beyond the acoustic limit.

6. **Phantom/target mismatch** — If your resolution target (wire, bead) has finite physical size or acoustic impedance contrast issues, measured resolution is convolved with target size.

7. **Speed of sound assumption** — Using 1540 m/s when your medium differs shifts depth calculations and blurs reconstructed images.

Check which of these applies by comparing your actual pulse spectrum and beam profile against your theoretical assumptions.
